passages.t: A camp with God in the middle
passages.happening:
The LORD tells Moses and Aaron how Israel is to camp. “The Israelites are to camp around the Tent of Meeting at a distance from it, each man under his standard, with the banners of his family” (verse 2).

On the east side, toward the sunrise, camps Judah, with Issachar and Zebulun. Their men number 186,400, and “they shall set out first” (verse 9). On the south camps Reuben, with Simeon and Gad. They set out second (verse 16).

Then comes the center. “In the middle of the camps, the Tent of Meeting is to travel with the camp of the Levites” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 1 answered the question how many. Chapter 2 answers where each one belongs. Before Israel takes a single step toward the promised land, the camp is shaped around one fact: God lives in the middle of his people.

A standard was a sign on a pole. It marked where a tribe camped and gathered, and smaller banners marked each family, so that every man knew which tents were his and where to fall in on the march. The chapter does not say what was on them. Later Jewish tradition imagined emblems, but the text gives none.

Ancient armies camped by rule. Egyptian carvings of the campaign of Ramesses II at Kadesh, about 1274 BC, show his camp as a rectangle with the king's tent in the center and his forces around it. Israel's camp follows a similar plan with one great difference. The tent in the middle belongs to no human king. The LORD is at the center, and the tribes are his army.

The east was the side of honor. The gate of the tabernacle's courtyard faced the sunrise (Exodus 27:13-16), and Moses and Aaron camped just before it (3:38). A hearer who knew the family's story would have noticed who holds that place. It is Judah, Jacob's fourth son, and not Reuben, the firstborn. That matches Jacob's last words, where Reuben loses his first place and the ruler's staff is promised to Judah (Genesis 49).

Verse 17 falls exactly between the first two camps and the last two. The list itself puts the tent in the middle.
passages.later:
Jacob had said of Judah, “The scepter will not depart from Judah, nor the staff from between his feet” (Genesis 49:10). The leader of Judah's camp, Nahshon, stands in the family line of David and of Jesus (Ruth 4:20; Matthew 1:4).

God had promised at Sinai, “Then I will dwell among the Israelites and be their God” (Exodus 29:45). John's Gospel takes up that promise: “The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us” (John 1:14). The Greek verb there means to pitch a tent.
passages.asks: Israel's whole camp took its shape from the tent at its center. Ask what sits at the center of your week, the thing everything else is arranged around. And ask what would have to move if God's presence were truly in the middle.

passages.happening:
On the west camps Ephraim, with Manasseh and Benjamin. They set out third (verse 24). On the north camps Dan, with Asher and Naphtali, and “they shall set out last, under their standards” (verse 31).

The total is given again: 603,550 (verse 32). The Levites are not counted among them (verse 33).

“So the Israelites did everything the LORD commanded Moses; they camped under their standards in this way and set out in the same way, each man with his clan and his family” (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
The grouping follows the family's history. Jacob's twelve sons had four mothers (Genesis 29 to 30 and 35). The east side holds three sons of Leah. The south holds Leah's first two sons with Gad, a son of her servant Zilpah. The west belongs to Rachel's line: Ephraim and Manasseh, the sons of Joseph, with Benjamin. The north gathers Dan and Naphtali, sons of Rachel's servant Bilhah, with Asher. An old and often painful family story has become the shape of a people. No branch of it is left out.

The same order holds on the march. The camp does not break into a crowd when it moves. Each tribe keeps its place, first, second, third and last, with the tent and the Levites in the middle of the line.

The chapter closes with the refrain of this part of the book: Israel did everything the LORD commanded. The words weigh more once chapters 11 to 14 have been read.

This ordered camp will be seen once more from outside. Much later a foreign seer, hired to curse Israel, will look down from a height, see ‘Israel encamped tribe by tribe’ (24:2), and find that he can only bless.
passages.later:
The Song of Songs uses this chapter's word for a standard: ‘his banner over me is love’ (Song of Songs 2:4).

The last pages of the Bible draw on the ordered camp. The new Jerusalem has the names of the twelve tribes on its gates: “There were three gates on the east, three on the north, three on the south, and three on the west” (Revelation 21:13). And a voice says, ‘Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man’ (Revelation 21:3). The link is one of theme, but the city John sees is built on the pattern of this camp.
passages.hard:
Could more than 600,000 fighting men, and perhaps two million people, really camp around one tent in the desert?

The difficulty is real. A camp that size would stretch for miles, and the desert could not feed it without constant provision, which is what the book describes.

Christians read the numbers in more than one way. Some take them as they stand, noting that the book presents Israel's survival as God's doing throughout and repeats the total in several places (1:46; 2:32; Exodus 38:26). Others note that the Hebrew word elef, usually ‘thousand’, can also mean a clan or a military unit, as when Gideon says, “my clan is the weakest in Manasseh” (Judges 6:15). George Mendenhall argued in 1958 that the tribal figures first recorded units and men, so that Judah's 74,600 would be seventy-four units totaling six hundred men. The main objection is that the chapter's own totals add the figures as thousands. Others again read the numbers as symbolic.

These notes take no side. The note on 1:20-46 and the note on Exodus 12:37 set out the question more fully. On every reading the chapter's point stands: the whole people is arranged around God's presence and moves only when he moves.
passages.asks: Every tribe had its own place, and no tribe was the center. Ask where you resent the place you have been given, in a family, a church or a job. And ask whether you have treated your own group as the middle of things, when the middle belongs to God.
